lessons.title: 1. What is Django?
lessons.html:
• Django = a Python web framework that lets you build web apps quickly with minimal code. Created 2003–2005.
  • It handles the boring parts: routing, database access, forms, admin panel — so you focus on your app logic.
  • Django is a back-end framework. It runs on the server, talks to the database, and sends HTML back to the browser.
  • Key idea: Django uses the MVT pattern — Model, View, Template — which is Django's version of MVC.

lessons.title: 2. MVT Architecture
lessons.html:
• Model = Python class mapped to a database table. Handles all data storage and retrieval (ORM).
  • View = Python function (or class) that receives an HTTP request, does logic, and returns an HTTP response. This is what MVC calls a Controller.
  • Template = HTML file with special Django tags. Generates the page the user sees. This is what MVC calls a View.
  • urls.py = the router — maps a URL to the right view.
  • Flow: Browser → urls.py → views.py → (optionally) Model + Template → HTTP response back to browser.
  • Trap: Django's "View" ≠ MVC's "View". In Django, the View is the logic layer (MVC Controller). The Template is the presentation layer (MVC View).

lessons.title: 3. Virtual Environment
lessons.html:
• Always work inside a virtual environment — an isolated Python installation just for your project. Avoids dependency conflicts between projects.
  • Create + activate:
    # create
python -m venv my_env
# activate (Linux/Mac)
source my_env/bin/activate
# activate (Windows)
my_env\Scripts\activate
  • Install Django:
    (my_env) $ python -m pip install django
  • Save dependencies:
    (my_env) $ pip freeze > requirements.txt
  • Trap: Never pip install without activating the venv first — you'll pollute the global Python.

lessons.title: 4. Create a Project
lessons.html:
• Create project:
    (my_env) $ django-admin startproject django_project .
    The . puts the files in the current folder instead of a nested folder.
  • Project anatomy:
    • manage.py — your command tool (runserver, migrate, startapp…)
    • settings.py — all configuration (INSTALLED_APPS, DATABASES, TEMPLATES…)
    • urls.py — the main URL router
    • wsgi.py — interface for traditional servers (Gunicorn, Apache)
    • asgi.py — interface for async servers (Channels, Daphne)
    • __init__.py — marks the folder as a Python package
  • Run the server:
    (my_env) $ python manage.py runserver
    Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000

lessons.title: 5. Create an App
lessons.html:
• A project = the whole website. An app = one feature/module inside the project. One project can have many apps (e.g. pages, meetings, blog).
  • Create app:
    (my_env) $ python manage.py startapp pages
  • Register it in settings.py:
    INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    'pages',  # add your app here
]
  • Trap: If you forget to add the app to INSTALLED_APPS, Django ignores it — models won't migrate, templates won't be found in some configs.

lessons.title: 6. First View
lessons.html:
• A view is a Python function that takes a request and returns a response.
  • The simplest response is HttpResponse:
    • from django.shortcuts import render
from django.http import HttpResponse

def home_page_view(request):
    return HttpResponse("Hello word")
  • The request object contains everything about the incoming HTTP request: method (GET/POST), user, headers, POST data.
  • Trap: Every view must return a response. Forgetting the return crashes with a ValueError.

lessons.title: 7. URL Routing
lessons.html:
• Django routes URLs in two steps: project urls.py → app urls.py.
  • App urls.py (create this file manually in your app folder):
    from django.urls import path
from .views import home_page_view

urlpatterns = [
    path('home/', home_page_view, name='home'),
]
  • Project urls.py — include the app's URLs:
    from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, include

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('pages/', include('pages.urls')),
]
  • Now visiting /pages/home/ calls home_page_view.
  • name= gives the URL a name so you can reverse it in templates: {% url 'home' %} instead of hardcoding /pages/home/.
  • Trap: include() takes a string 'pages.urls', not pages.urls.

lessons.title: 1. Multi-App Project Structure
lessons.html:
• The Meeting Planner project has two apps: website (home + about pages) and meetings (the meeting data).
  • Structure:
    meetings_planner/
  meetings/          ← app: meetings logic
  meetings_planner/  ← project config folder
  website/           ← app: public pages
  manage.py
  • Each app gets registered in INSTALLED_APPS:
    INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    'website',
    'meetings',
]
  • Each app has its own urls.py. The project's urls.py includes both.

lessons.title: 2. render() and Templates
lessons.html:
• Instead of returning raw text with HttpResponse, real views use render() to send an HTML template.
    • from django.shortcuts import render

def home_view(request):
    return render(request, 'website/home.html')
  • render(request, template_name, context) — the third argument is a context dict: data you want to use in the template.
    • def home_view(request):
    context = {'meetings': Meeting.objects.all()}
    return render(request, 'website/home.html', context=context)
  • Template location: put HTML files at appname/templates/appname/filename.html. The double appname/ avoids name clashes between apps.
  • Trap: If you put templates directly in appname/templates/ without the sub-folder, two apps both having home.html will clash — Django picks one unpredictably.

lessons.title: 3. URL Parameters
lessons.html:
• To capture a value from the URL (like a meeting ID), use angle brackets in the path:
    • path('meetings/<int:id>/', views.detail, name='detail')
  • Django passes id as a keyword argument to the view:
    • def detail(request, id):
    meeting = Meeting.objects.get(pk=id)
    return render(request, 'meetings/detail.html', {'meeting': meeting})
  • Type converters: <int:id> matches integers only. Others: <str:slug>, <slug:slug>, <uuid:id>.
  • Trap: Using Meeting.objects.get(pk=id) raises Meeting.DoesNotExist if the ID doesn't exist — your app crashes. Use get_object_or_404 instead (see next lesson).

lessons.title: 4. get_object_or_404
lessons.html:
• get_object_or_404 is the safe way to look up an object by ID. If nothing is found, it returns a proper 404 page instead of crashing.
    • from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404, render
from .models import Meeting

def detail(request, id):
    meeting = get_object_or_404(Meeting, id=id)
    return render(request, 'meetings/detail.html', {'meeting': meeting})
  • Import it from django.shortcuts (same place as render).
  • Rule of thumb: Always use get_object_or_404 in views when looking up by user-supplied ID. Use .get() only in internal scripts where you're sure the object exists.

lessons.title: 5. Template Language Basics
lessons.html:
• Django templates are HTML files with extra syntax:
  • Display a variable: {{ variable }}
  • Tags (logic): {% tag %}
  • Filters: {{ variable|filtername }}
  • For loop:
    <ul>
{% for meeting in meetings %}
  <li>{{ meeting.title }}</li>
{% endfor %}
</ul>
  • If/else:
    {% if meetings %}
  <p>{{ meetings|length }} meetings</p>
{% else %}
  <p>No meetings yet.</p>
{% endif %}
  • Comments: {# this is a comment #} or {% comment %}...{% endcomment %}
  • Link to a named URL: <a href="{% url 'detail' meeting.id %}">
  • Trap: Django template syntax uses {% %} not <% %> (that's other frameworks). And {{ }} for output, not <%= %>.

lessons.title: 6. Template Inheritance
lessons.html:
• Inheritance lets you define a base template with the common layout (navbar, footer, CSS) and child templates that just fill in the unique content. No copy-pasting HTML.
  • base.html:
    <!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>{% block title %}{% endblock %}</title>
</head>
<body>
  {% block content %}
  {% endblock %}
</body>
</html>
  • about.html (child):
    {% extends "base.html" %}
{% block title %}About{% endblock %}
{% block content %}
  <h2>Meeting Planner — Tek-up</h2>
{% endblock %}
  • Traps: {% extends %} must be the very first line of the child template. Any HTML before it is silently ignored. Block names must match exactly.
  • {% include %} is different — it inserts a template fragment (like a navbar snippet) without inheritance. Use {% include 'navbar.html' %}.

lessons.title: 7. Static Files
lessons.html:
• Static files = CSS, JavaScript, images. Django serves them from each app's static/ folder during development.
  • In settings.py: STATIC_URL = 'static/' (already there by default).
  • In your template, load the tag first, then use it:
    {% load static %}
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet"
        href="{% static 'website/style.css' %}">
</head>
  • File lives at: website/static/website/style.css
  • Trap: Forgetting {% load static %} at the top of the template causes a TemplateSyntaxError: Invalid block tag 'static'.
  • STATIC_ROOT = where collectstatic gathers all static files for production deployment. Not needed during development.

lessons.title: 1. What is a Model?
lessons.html:
• A model is a Python class that maps to a database table. Each attribute = one column. Django generates all the SQL for you.
  • All models inherit from models.Model.
  • The mapping: class → table, attribute → column, instance → row.
  • You never write CREATE TABLE — Django does it via migrations.
  • Models also power the Admin panel and ModelForms — one definition, three uses.

lessons.title: 2. Field Types
lessons.html:
• CharField(max_length=N) — short text. max_length is required.
  • TextField() — long text, no max_length needed.
  • IntegerField() — whole numbers.
  • DecimalField(max_digits=N, decimal_places=N) — exact decimals. Use for money, not FloatField.
  • DateField() — a date. DateTimeField() — date + time. TimeField() — time only.
  • EmailField() — like CharField but validates email format.
  • BooleanField() — True/False.
  • Trap: CharField without max_length raises a system check error. TextField does not need it.

lessons.title: 3. Field Options
lessons.html:
• default=value — used if you don't supply one: duration = models.IntegerField(default=1).
  • null=True — allows NULL in the database column.
  • blank=True — allows the field to be empty in a form.
  • null is a database concept. blank is a form-validation concept. They are independent.
  • auto_now_add=True — sets the value to now when first created. Read-only after that.
  • Trap: Do not use null=True on a CharField/TextField — you'll have both NULL and '' as 'empty', making queries inconsistent.

lessons.title: 4. __str__ method
lessons.html:
• __str__ controls how an object is displayed as text — in the admin panel, in print(), and in {{ object }} in templates.
  • Without it, Django shows Meeting object (1) — useless.
  • Professor's example (verified output: Réunion at 09:00:00 on 2027-01-15):
    def __str__(self):
    return f"{self.title} at {self.start_time} on {self.date}"
  • Trap: __str__ must return a string. Returning an integer raises TypeError.

lessons.title: 5. The Migration Workflow
lessons.html:
• Migrations = Python scripts that describe database schema changes.
  • 3-step workflow — always in this order:
    1. Change your model in models.py
    2. python manage.py makemigrations — generates the script
    3. python manage.py migrate — runs the script on the database
  • Trap: Editing models.py does NOT change the database automatically. Forgetting migrate causes OperationalError: no such column.

lessons.title: 6. Migration Commands
lessons.html:
• python manage.py makemigrations — generates a new migration file in migrations/.
  • python manage.py migrate — applies all pending migrations to the database.
  • python manage.py showmigrations — lists all migrations: [X] applied, [ ] pending.
  • python manage.py sqlmigrate meetings 0001 — shows the actual SQL without running it. Good for understanding and debugging.
  • Real output from the professor's project:
    $ python manage.py showmigrations meetings
meetings
 [X] 0001_initial

lessons.title: 7. Professor's Models — Meeting Planner
lessons.html:
• These are the exact models from the professor's slides — verified running in Django 5.1:
    • from django.db import models
from datetime import time

class Room(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=50)
    floor = models.IntegerField()
    room_number = models.IntegerField()
    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.name}: room {self.room_number} on floor {self.floor}"

class Meeting(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    date = models.DateField()
    start_time = models.TimeField(default=time(9))
    duration = models.IntegerField(default=1)
    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.title} at {self.start_time} on {self.date}"
  • Verified: str(room) → Salle A: room 201 on floor 2
  • Verified: str(meeting) → Réunion at 09:00:00 on 2027-01-15

lessons.title: 1. What is the Admin Panel?
lessons.html:
• Django's built-in admin interface gives you a full CRUD web UI for your models — generated automatically, no HTML needed.
  • It's the back-office for staff, not for end-users.
  • Access at http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/ after creating a superuser.
  • Built on django.contrib.admin which is in INSTALLED_APPS by default.
  • The URL is wired up by default: path('admin/', admin.site.urls).

lessons.title: 2. Register a Model
lessons.html:
• To make a model appear in the admin, register it in admin.py:
    • from django.contrib import admin
from .models import Meeting

admin.site.register(Meeting)
  • That's it. Django generates the full list, add, edit, and delete views automatically.
  • Trap: If you forget to register a model, it simply won't appear — no error. Easy to miss.

lessons.title: 3. Create a Superuser
lessons.html:
• Only users with is_staff=True or is_superuser=True can log into the admin.
  • Create the first superuser with:
    python manage.py createsuperuser
  • Django prompts for username, email, and password.
  • Trap: Run migrate first. Running createsuperuser before migrate gives no such table: auth_user.

lessons.title: 4. __str__ in the Admin
lessons.html:
• Without __str__, the admin lists your objects as Meeting object (1), Meeting object (2)…
  • With __str__, it shows meaningful names: Réunion at 09:00:00 on 2027-01-15.
  • Always define __str__ on every model — it affects the admin, the shell, and templates.

lessons.title: 5. Customising Admin (ModelAdmin)
lessons.html:
• To customise how a model appears, create a ModelAdmin class:
    • from django.contrib import admin
from .models import Meeting

@admin.register(Meeting)
class MeetingAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    list_display  = ['title', 'date', 'start_time', 'duration']
    list_filter   = ['date']
    search_fields = ['title']
  • list_display — columns in the list view.
  • list_filter — sidebar filter panel.
  • search_fields — adds a search box.
  • @admin.register(Meeting) = same as admin.site.register(Meeting, MeetingAdmin) — just shorter.
  • Trap: Typos in list_display cause ImproperlyConfigured errors.

lessons.title: 1. Why model relations?
lessons.html:
• Real data has relationships. A Meeting belongs to a Room. A Book belongs to an Author. A Student can enroll in many Courses.
  • Django has three relationship field types that map directly to database foreign keys and join tables: ForeignKey, OneToOneField, ManyToManyField.
  • You define the relationship in Python — Django generates all the SQL.

lessons.title: 2. ForeignKey — one-to-many
lessons.html:
• Use ForeignKey when many objects belong to one parent. One Room → many Meetings. One Author → many Books.
  • Defined on the many side:
    • class Meeting(models.Model):
    room = models.ForeignKey(Room, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
  • Forward access (meeting → room): meeting.room.name
  • Reverse access (room → all its meetings): room.meeting_set.all()
  • Django auto-creates the reverse accessor named modelname_set. Use related_name='meetings' to rename it: room.meetings.all()
  • Trap: on_delete is required. Missing it raises TypeError.

lessons.title: 3. on_delete options
lessons.html:
• on_delete tells Django what to do when the parent is deleted.
  • models.CASCADE — delete all children. If Room is deleted → all its Meetings are deleted. Most common.
  • models.SET_NULL — set the FK to NULL. Requires null=True on the field. Meeting stays but meeting.room becomes None.
  • models.PROTECT — prevent deletion. If a Room has Meetings, you cannot delete the Room (raises ProtectedError).
  • models.SET_DEFAULT — set FK to the field's default value.
  • models.DO_NOTHING — do nothing. Dangerous — can break referential integrity.
  • Trap: SET_NULL without null=True on the field causes a database error.

lessons.title: 4. OneToOneField
lessons.html:
• Use OneToOneField when each object is linked to exactly one other. One User → one Profile.
    • class Profile(models.Model):
    user = models.OneToOneField(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    bio = models.TextField()
  • Forward: profile.user.username
  • Reverse: user.profile — Django creates a reverse accessor automatically (not profile_set — just profile since it's one-to-one).
  • Use case: extend the built-in User model without modifying it.
  • Trap: Accessing user.profile when no Profile exists raises RelatedObjectDoesNotExist.

lessons.title: 5. ManyToManyField
lessons.html:
• Use ManyToManyField when many objects relate to many others. A Student can enroll in many Courses. A Course has many Students.
    • class Course(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)

class Student(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    courses = models.ManyToManyField(Course)
  • Django automatically creates an intermediate join table (e.g. student_courses) — you don't define it.
  • Add: student.courses.add(course)
  • Remove: student.courses.remove(course)
  • Query: student.courses.all()
  • Trap: M2M fields must be defined on one side only. Django handles both directions.

lessons.title: 6. related_name
lessons.html:
• related_name customises the reverse accessor name on the parent model.
    • class Meeting(models.Model):
    room = models.ForeignKey(Room,
        on_delete=models.CASCADE,
        related_name='meetings')  # instead of meeting_set
  • Now: room.meetings.all() instead of room.meeting_set.all()
  • Useful when a model has two FKs to the same model — without related_name Django raises a clash error.
  • Also used to suppress the reverse accessor: related_name='+' (no reverse access).

lessons.title: 7. Professor's Meeting + Room relation
lessons.html:
• From the professor's slides — the final Meeting model with the Room ForeignKey (verified running):
    • class Meeting(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    date = models.DateField()
    start_time = models.TimeField(default=time(9))
    duration = models.IntegerField(default=1)
    room = models.ForeignKey(Room, on_delete=models.CASCADE)

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.title} at {self.start_time} on {self.date}"
  • Verified: m.room.name → 'Conf A'
  • Verified: r.meeting_set.all() → all meetings in that room
  • Verified: deleting a Room → all its Meetings are deleted (CASCADE)

lessons.title: 1. Template language overview
lessons.html:
• Django templates are HTML files with extra syntax. Three types of constructs:
  • {{ variable }} — outputs a value from the context.
  • {% tag %} — logic: loops, conditions, inheritance, loading tag libraries.
  • {{ variable|filter }} — transforms a value before displaying it.
  • {# comment #} — single-line comment (not sent to browser).
  • Everything else is plain HTML — Django passes it through unchanged.
  • Trap: Django uses {% %} not <% %> (that is PHP/ASP/ERB). And {{ }} not <%= %>.

lessons.title: 2. for and empty
lessons.html:
• Loop over a list from the context:
    • {% for meeting in meetings %}
  <li>{{ meeting.title }}</li>
{% empty %}
  <li>No meetings yet.</li>
{% endfor %}
  • {% empty %} runs when the list is empty — saves an extra {% if %}.
  • Inside the loop: {{ forloop.counter }} (1-based), {{ forloop.counter0 }} (0-based), {{ forloop.first }}, {{ forloop.last }}.
  • Trap: Forgetting {% endfor %} causes a TemplateSyntaxError.

lessons.title: 3. if, elif, else
lessons.html:
• Conditional logic:
    • {% if user.is_authenticated %}
  <p>Hello, {{ user.username }}!</p>
{% elif user.is_staff %}
  <p>Admin area</p>
{% else %}
  <p>Please log in.</p>
{% endif %}
  • Operators: ==, !=, <, >, in, not in, and, or, not.
  • Trap: Django templates do not support arbitrary Python expressions inside {% if %}. Keep logic simple — move complex conditions to the view.

lessons.title: 4. url and csrf_token
lessons.html:
• {% url 'name' %} — generates a URL by name (reverse), so paths never get hardcoded:
    • <a href="{% url 'detail' meeting.id %}">View</a>
<!-- generates: /meetings/5/ -->
  • {% csrf_token %} — required inside every POST form. Protects against Cross-Site Request Forgery attacks. Without it, Django returns a 403 Forbidden error on form submission.
    • <form method="post">
  {% csrf_token %}
  {{ form.as_p }}
  <button type="submit">Save</button>
</form>
  • Trap: Forgetting {% csrf_token %} in a POST form → 403 error. This was question 1 on the actual exam.

lessons.title: 5. extends, block, include
lessons.html:
• {% extends %} — inherit a base template. Must be the first line of the child template.
  • {% block name %}{% endblock %} — a named hole in the base; children fill it in.
  • {% include 'fragment.html' %} — insert another template inline (no inheritance).
    • 
<html>
<head><title>{% block title %}{% endblock %}</title></head>
<body>{% block content %}{% endblock %}</body>
</html>


{% extends "base.html" %}
{% block title %}Home{% endblock %}
{% block content %}
  <h1>Welcome</h1>
{% endblock %}
  • Traps: {% extends %} must be line 1. Block names must match exactly. A child cannot add content outside blocks.

lessons.title: 6. load static and static files
lessons.html:
• To link CSS/JS/images, use the static template tag:
    • {% load static %}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'website/style.css' %}">
<img src="{% static 'website/logo.png' %}">
  • File must exist at: appname/static/appname/filename
  • Setting in settings.py: STATIC_URL = 'static/'
  • For production: python manage.py collectstatic gathers all files into STATIC_ROOT.
  • Trap: Forgetting {% load static %} before {% static %} → TemplateSyntaxError: Invalid block tag 'static'.

lessons.title: 7. Filters
lessons.html:
• Filters transform a value: {{ value|filtername }} or {{ value|filtername:arg }}.
  • {{ name|upper }} → MALAK
  • {{ name|lower }} → malak
  • {{ items|length }} → 3
  • {{ text|truncatechars:10 }} → Hello wor…
  • {{ value|default:'N/A' }} → shows 'N/A' if value is empty/falsy
  • {{ date|date:'d/m/Y' }} → 15/01/2027
  • {{ html|safe }} → renders HTML tags (don't use on user input!)
  • Chain filters: {{ name|lower|truncatechars:20 }}
  • Trap: {{ text|safe }} on untrusted user input = XSS vulnerability. Only use |safe on content you control.

lessons.title: 1. Why forms matter
lessons.html:
• Forms are how users send data to Django. Every login box, search bar, and contact page is a form.
  • Django provides three layers: raw HTML <form> (Method 1), forms.Form (Method 2), and forms.ModelForm (Method 3).
  • Method 1 is the least code but the most dangerous — no validation, no CSRF by default if you forget the tag.
  • Method 2 adds field-level validation and cleans data for you via form.cleaned_data.
  • Method 3 ties directly to a model and can create/update database rows with a single form.save().
  • Trap: Every POST form in Django must include {% csrf_token %} inside the <form> tag, or Django returns 403 Forbidden.

lessons.title: 2. Method 1 — raw POST data
lessons.html:
• The simplest approach: read request.POST['fieldname'] directly in the view.
    • def contact_view(request):
    if request.method == 'POST':
        firstname = request.POST['firstname']
        Contact.objects.create(
            firstname=firstname,
            lastname=request.POST['lastname'],
            email=request.POST['email'],
            message=request.POST['message']
        )
        return redirect('home')
    return render(request, 'contact/contact.html')
  • The HTML form must have method="post" and each input must have a name attribute that matches request.POST['name'].
  • Trap: request.POST['key'] raises KeyError if the field is missing. Use request.POST.get('key', '') for optional fields.

lessons.title: 3. Method 2 — forms.Form
lessons.html:
• Define a form class in forms.py:
    • from django import forms

class ContactForm(forms.Form):
    firstname = forms.CharField(max_length=10)
    lastname  = forms.CharField(max_length=10)
    email     = forms.EmailField()
    msg       = forms.CharField(widget=forms.Textarea)
  • Use it in the view:
    • def contact_view(request):
    form = ContactForm(request.POST or None)
    if form.is_valid():
        data = form.cleaned_data
        Contact.objects.create(
            firstname=data['firstname'],
            lastname=data['lastname'],
            email=data['email'],
            message=data['msg']
        )
        return redirect('home')
    return render(request, 'contact.html', {'form': form})
  • form.is_valid() runs all field validators. form.cleaned_data gives you safe, converted Python values (not raw strings).
  • Trap: Never access form.cleaned_data before calling is_valid() — it raises AttributeError.

lessons.title: 4. Method 3 — forms.ModelForm
lessons.html:
• A ModelForm generates form fields automatically from a model. Much less code than Method 2.
    • from django import forms
from .models import Contact

class ContactModelForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Contact
        fields = ['firstname', 'lastname', 'email', 'message']
  • Use it in the view — form.save() creates the database row:
    • def contact_view(request):
    form = ContactModelForm(request.POST or None)
    if form.is_valid():
        form.save()
        return redirect('home')
    return render(request, 'contact.html', {'form': form})
  • fields = '__all__' includes every model field. Explicit list is safer.
  • Trap: Using fields = '__all__' in production can expose sensitive fields. Always list fields explicitly.

lessons.title: 5. Rendering forms in templates
lessons.html:
• Three built-in render helpers:
  • {{ form.as_p }} — wraps each field in a <p> tag. Most common.
  • {{ form.as_table }} — wraps in <tr> tags. Needs an outer <table>.
  • {{ form.as_ul }} — wraps in <li> tags. Needs outer <ul>.
  • Minimal form template:
    • <form method="post">
  {% csrf_token %}
  {{ form.as_p }}
  <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>
  • Display errors: {{ form.errors }} or per-field: {{ form.firstname.errors }}.
  • Trap: Forgetting method="post" on the HTML form tag — the browser sends a GET and request.POST is empty.

lessons.title: 6. Custom validation
lessons.html:
• Add custom validation by defining a clean_<fieldname> method on the form class.
    • from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError
import datetime

class MeetingForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Meeting
        fields = '__all__'

    def clean_date(self):
        date = self.cleaned_data['date']
        if date < datetime.date.today():
            raise ValidationError("Meeting date must be in the future.")
        return date
  • clean_<field> must return the cleaned value or raise ValidationError.
  • For cross-field validation, override clean(self) (without field suffix).
  • Trap: Forgetting to return date at the end of clean_date() sets the field to None in cleaned_data.

lessons.title: 7. Widgets
lessons.html:
• A widget controls how a form field is rendered as HTML. Each field type has a default widget.
  • Override a widget in the form field definition:
    • class ContactForm(forms.Form):
    msg = forms.CharField(widget=forms.Textarea)
    date = forms.DateField(widget=forms.SelectDateWidget)
  • Or override in a ModelForm's Meta:
    • class MeetingForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Meeting
        fields = '__all__'
        widgets = {
            'date': forms.SelectDateWidget,
        }
  • Common widgets: TextInput, Textarea, Select, CheckboxInput, DateInput, SelectDateWidget, PasswordInput.
  • Trap: widget=forms.Textarea (the class), not widget=forms.Textarea() in Meta.widgets — both actually work, but be consistent with your codebase.

lessons.title: 1. The QuerySet
lessons.html:
• A QuerySet is a lazy collection of database rows. It is built up in Python and only hits the database when you evaluate it (iterate, convert to list, call len(), slice, etc.).
  • Every model's manager — Model.objects — is the starting point for all queries.
  • QuerySets are lazy: Room.objects.filter(floor=1) does NOT query the database immediately. The SQL runs only when you use the result.
  • QuerySets are chainable: each method returns a new QuerySet.
    • rooms = Room.objects.filter(floor=1).order_by('name')[:5]
  • Trap: Calling len(queryset) evaluates the entire queryset. Use queryset.count() for counts — it runs SELECT COUNT(*) which is much faster.

lessons.title: 2. Retrieving objects — all, filter, get
lessons.html:
• Room.objects.all() — returns all rows as a QuerySet.
  • Room.objects.filter(floor=1) — returns rows matching the condition.
  • Room.objects.get(pk=1) — returns exactly one row. Raises DoesNotExist if not found, MultipleObjectsReturned if more than one matches.
    • # all rooms
rooms = Room.objects.all()

# filter by field
floor1 = Room.objects.filter(floor=1)

# get one (raises exception if not found)
room = Room.objects.get(pk=5)
  • Trap: .get() in a view without try/except crashes with an unhandled exception. Use get_object_or_404 instead.

lessons.title: 3. Field lookups
lessons.html:
• Field lookups are appended to field names with double underscores: field__lookup=value.
  • __exact — exact match (default). filter(name='Conf A') = filter(name__exact='Conf A').
  • __iexact — case-insensitive exact match.
  • __contains — SQL LIKE '%value%'. __icontains — case-insensitive.
  • __startswith, __endswith — prefix/suffix match.
  • __gt, __gte, __lt, __lte — greater/less than comparisons.
  • __in — value in a list: filter(floor__in=[1,2]).
  • __isnull — filter(room__isnull=True).
    • Meeting.objects.filter(title__icontains='django')
Meeting.objects.filter(duration__gte=2)
Room.objects.filter(floor__in=[1, 2])
  • Trap: Using filter(name='conf a') does a case-sensitive match and misses 'Conf A'. Use __iexact for user-facing searches.

lessons.title: 4. Ordering, slicing, counting
lessons.html:
• .order_by('name') — ascending. .order_by('-name') — descending (prefix with -).
  • Default ordering can be set on the model's Meta class and applies automatically.
  • Slicing a QuerySet maps to SQL LIMIT/OFFSET:
    • first5 = Room.objects.all()[:5]       # LIMIT 5
skip2  = Room.objects.all()[2:7]      # OFFSET 2 LIMIT 5
  • .count() returns an integer via SELECT COUNT(*) — does not load rows into memory.
  • .exists() returns True/False — the fastest way to check if any row matches.
    • n = Room.objects.count()
has_rooms = Room.objects.filter(floor=5).exists()
  • Trap: Negative slicing (queryset[-1]) is not supported — raises AssertionError. Use .order_by('-pk')[0] instead.

lessons.title: 5. Creating, updating, deleting
lessons.html:
• Create — two ways:
    • # Option A: create() — one step
r = Room.objects.create(name='Lab 1', floor=3, room_number=301)

# Option B: instantiate + save()
r = Room(name='Lab 1', floor=3, room_number=301)
r.save()
  • Update a single object:
    • r = Room.objects.get(pk=1)
r.name = 'Main Hall'
r.save()
  • Bulk update (SQL UPDATE in one query):
    • Room.objects.filter(floor=5).update(floor=4)
  • Delete a single object:
    • r = Room.objects.get(pk=1)
r.delete()
  • Bulk delete:
    • Room.objects.filter(floor=99).delete()
  • Trap: .update() and .delete() on a QuerySet bypass model save() signals and __str__. If you rely on those signals, loop and call .save()/.delete() individually.

lessons.title: 6. values(), exclude(), select_related()
lessons.html:
• .values('field1', 'field2') — returns a QuerySet of dicts instead of model instances. Useful for lightweight reads:
    • Room.objects.values('name', 'floor')
# [{'name': 'Conf A', 'floor': 1}, ...]
  • .exclude(condition) — the opposite of .filter():
    • Room.objects.exclude(floor=1)  # all rooms NOT on floor 1
  • .select_related('fk_field') — fetches related ForeignKey objects in a single SQL JOIN. Avoids the N+1 query problem.
    • # Without select_related: 1 query per meeting to fetch room
meetings = Meeting.objects.all()  # N+1 queries

# With select_related: 1 query total
meetings = Meeting.objects.select_related('room').all()
  • Trap: Forgetting select_related when looping over meetings and accessing meeting.room causes one SQL query per row — the N+1 problem.

lessons.title: 7. DoesNotExist and get_object_or_404
lessons.html:
• Model.DoesNotExist is raised by .get() when no row matches. It's defined on every model automatically.
    • try:
    room = Room.objects.get(pk=99999)
except Room.DoesNotExist:
    # handle missing room
    pass
  • get_object_or_404 is the view-layer shortcut: returns the object or raises an Http404 (which renders a 404 page):
    • from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404

def room_detail(request, pk):
    room = get_object_or_404(Room, pk=pk)
    return render(request, 'meetings/detail.html', {'room': room})
  • Combining filter + get_object_or_404:
    • meeting = get_object_or_404(Meeting, pk=pk, room__floor=1)
  • Trap: DoesNotExist is on the model class — it's Room.DoesNotExist, not a global exception. Catching the wrong exception silently ignores it.

chapters.title: Class-Based Views — ListView, CreateView, UpdateView, DeleteView

lessons.title: 1. What are Class-Based Views?
lessons.html:
• A Class-Based View (CBV) is a view written as a Python class instead of a function. Django provides built-in generic CBVs that handle the most common patterns (list, detail, create, update, delete) with almost no code.
  • Function-based view (FBV) vs Class-Based View (CBV):
    # FBV
def post_list(request):
    posts = BlogPost.objects.all()
    return render(request, 'blog/list.html', {'posts': posts})

# CBV — same result
class PostListView(ListView):
    model = BlogPost
    template_name = 'blog/list.html'
    context_object_name = 'posts'
  • CBVs are wired into urls.py using .as_view():
    path('posts/', PostListView.as_view(), name='post-list')
  • Trap: Forgetting .as_view() in urls.py passes the class itself, not a callable view — Django raises a TypeError at runtime.

lessons.title: 2. ListView
lessons.html:
• ListView fetches all rows of a model and passes them to a template.
    • from django.views.generic import ListView
from .models import BlogPost

class PostListView(ListView):
    model = BlogPost
    template_name = 'blog/post_list.html'
    context_object_name = 'posts'
  • Default template: if you omit template_name, Django looks for <app>/<model>_list.html — e.g. blog/blogpost_list.html.
  • Default context name: if you omit context_object_name, Django uses <model>_list — e.g. blogpost_list. With context_object_name = 'posts', the template uses {% for post in posts %}.
  • Override queryset: override get_queryset() to filter or order:
    def get_queryset(self):
    return BlogPost.objects.filter(author=self.request.user).order_by('-created_on')
  • Trap: Setting queryset = BlogPost.objects.all() as a class attribute is evaluated once at class definition — changes after startup won't reflect. Use get_queryset() for dynamic queries.

lessons.title: 3. DetailView
lessons.html:
• DetailView fetches a single object by its primary key (from the URL) and passes it to a template.
    • from django.views.generic import DetailView

class PostDetailView(DetailView):
    model = BlogPost
    context_object_name = 'post'
    template_name = 'blog/post_detail.html'
  • URL must pass <int:pk> (or <int:id> with extra config):
    path('posts/<int:pk>/', PostDetailView.as_view(), name='post-detail')
  • Default template: <app>/<model>_detail.html.
  • Default context name: object (or <model> lowercase — both are available).
  • Trap: If the URL uses <int:id> instead of <int:pk>, you must override pk_url_kwarg = 'id' on the view, otherwise Django raises a 404.

lessons.title: 4. CreateView
lessons.html:
• CreateView displays a form on GET and saves a new model instance on POST.
    • from django.views.generic import CreateView
from django.urls import reverse_lazy

class PostCreateView(CreateView):
    model = BlogPost
    fields = ['title', 'content', 'author']
    template_name = 'blog/post_form.html'
    success_url = reverse_lazy('post-list')
  • fields — which model fields to include in the form. Use '__all__' to include everything.
  • success_url — where to redirect after a successful save. Use reverse_lazy() (not reverse()) because URLs aren't loaded yet when the class is defined.
  • Default template: <app>/<model>_form.html.
  • Trap: Using reverse() instead of reverse_lazy() in a class attribute raises NoReverseMatch at import time — before urls.py is loaded.

lessons.title: 5. UpdateView
lessons.html:
• UpdateView loads an existing object by pk, displays it in a form, and saves changes on POST.
    • from django.views.generic import UpdateView

class PostUpdateView(UpdateView):
    model = BlogPost
    fields = ['title', 'content']
    template_name = 'blog/post_form.html'
    success_url = reverse_lazy('post-list')
  • It shares the same form template as CreateView by convention (post_form.html). The form is pre-filled with the existing data.
  • URL needs <int:pk>:
    path('posts/<int:pk>/edit/', PostUpdateView.as_view(), name='post-update')
  • Trap: Omitting success_url and not defining get_absolute_url() on the model causes ImproperlyConfigured after save.

lessons.title: 6. DeleteView
lessons.html:
• DeleteView shows a confirmation page on GET and deletes the object on POST.
    • from django.views.generic import DeleteView

class PostDeleteView(DeleteView):
    model = BlogPost
    template_name = 'blog/post_confirm_delete.html'
    success_url = reverse_lazy('post-list')
  • Default template: <app>/<model>_confirm_delete.html.
  • The confirmation template just needs a POST form with a submit button:
    <form method="post">
  {% csrf_token %}
  <p>Delete "{{ object.title }}"?</p>
  <button type="submit">Yes, delete</button>
</form>
  • URL needs <int:pk>:
    path('posts/<int:pk>/delete/', PostDeleteView.as_view(), name='post-delete')
  • Trap: A GET request to DeleteView does NOT delete anything — it shows the confirmation page. Only a POST triggers deletion.

lessons.title: 7. LoginRequiredMixin
lessons.html:
• LoginRequiredMixin protects a CBV — anonymous users are redirected to the login page.
    • from django.contrib.auth.mixins import LoginRequiredMixin
from django.views.generic import CreateView

class PostCreateView(LoginRequiredMixin, CreateView):
    model = BlogPost
    fields = ['title', 'content']
    success_url = reverse_lazy('post-list')
  • Mixin order matters: LoginRequiredMixin must come first in the class definition, before the view class. Python's MRO runs left to right.
  • For function-based views the equivalent is the @login_required decorator:
    from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required

@login_required
def my_view(request):
    ...
  • Trap: Putting LoginRequiredMixin after the view class (class MyView(CreateView, LoginRequiredMixin)) silently fails — the mixin's dispatch() override never runs.

chapters.title: Authentication — User model, login, signup, permissions

lessons.title: 1. The built-in User model
lessons.html:
• Django ships with a complete authentication system. The User model lives in django.contrib.auth.models.
  • Key fields:
    • username — unique, required
    • password — stored as a hash, never plain text
    • email, first_name, last_name
    • is_active — False = account disabled
    • is_staff — True = can access the admin panel
    • is_superuser — True = all permissions, no checks
  • Create a user in code:
    from django.contrib.auth.models import User
u = User.objects.create_user(
    username='malak',
    password='secret123',
    email='m@example.com'
)
  • Trap: Never use User.objects.create(password='plain') — it stores the password as plain text. Always use create_user() which hashes the password.

lessons.title: 2. authenticate() and login()
lessons.html:
• authenticate(username, password) checks credentials. Returns the User object if valid, None if not.
  • login(request, user) creates a session so the user stays logged in across requests.
    • from django.contrib.auth import authenticate, login

def login_view(request):
    if request.method == 'POST':
        username = request.POST['username']
        password = request.POST['password']
        user = authenticate(request, username=username, password=password)
        if user is not None:
            login(request, user)
            return redirect('home')
        else:
            return render(request, 'login.html', {'error': 'Invalid credentials'})
    return render(request, 'login.html')
  • Trap: Calling login(request, user) without first calling authenticate() skips the credential check — anyone can be logged in. Always authenticate first.

lessons.title: 3. logout()
lessons.html:
• logout(request) clears the session and logs the user out.
    • from django.contrib.auth import logout

def logout_view(request):
    logout(request)
    return redirect('home')
  • After calling logout(), request.user becomes an AnonymousUser.
  • The logout URL should only accept POST requests (to prevent CSRF logout attacks via a link):
    # urls.py
path('logout/', views.logout_view, name='logout')

# template
<form method="post" action="{% url 'logout' %}">
  {% csrf_token %}
  <button>Log out</button>
</form>
  • Trap: Using a GET link <a href="/logout/"> to logout makes the site vulnerable to logout CSRF — an attacker can embed an invisible image that logs the user out.

lessons.title: 4. Signup — creating users
lessons.html:
• Django provides UserCreationForm — a built-in ModelForm that creates a new user with password confirmation.
    • from django.contrib.auth.forms import UserCreationForm
from django.contrib.auth import login

def signup_view(request):
    form = UserCreationForm(request.POST or None)
    if form.is_valid():
        user = form.save()         # hashes password, saves user
        login(request, user)       # log in immediately
        return redirect('home')
    return render(request, 'signup.html', {'form': form})
  • UserCreationForm validates that the two password fields match and that the password meets Django's strength requirements.
  • To add extra fields (email, first name), extend it:
    class SignupForm(UserCreationForm):
    email = forms.EmailField(required=True)
    class Meta:
        model = User
        fields = ['username', 'email', 'password1', 'password2']
  • Trap: Calling User.objects.create(password=form.cleaned_data['password1']) stores the password in plain text. form.save() handles hashing correctly.

lessons.title: 5. @login_required and LoginRequiredMixin
lessons.html:
• Both tools redirect anonymous users to the login page. Choose based on whether the view is a function or a class.
  • Function-based: use the @login_required decorator:
    from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required

@login_required
def dashboard(request):
    return render(request, 'dashboard.html')
  • Anonymous users are redirected to settings.LOGIN_URL (default: /accounts/login/). The original URL is passed as ?next=/dashboard/ so users land back after login.
  • Class-based: use LoginRequiredMixin as the first base class:
    from django.contrib.auth.mixins import LoginRequiredMixin

class DashboardView(LoginRequiredMixin, ListView):
    model = BlogPost
    context_object_name = 'posts'
  • Trap: @login_required works on functions only. Applying it to a CBV's class (not .as_view()) does nothing. Use LoginRequiredMixin for CBVs.

lessons.title: 6. request.user and is_authenticated
lessons.html:
• In every view, request.user is set by Django's AuthenticationMiddleware.
  • If the user is logged in: request.user is a User instance and request.user.is_authenticated is True.
  • If not logged in: request.user is AnonymousUser and is_authenticated is False.
  • Use it in views:
    def home(request):
    if request.user.is_authenticated:
        posts = BlogPost.objects.filter(author=request.user)
    else:
        posts = BlogPost.objects.none()
    return render(request, 'home.html', {'posts': posts})
  • Use it in templates:
    {% if user.is_authenticated %}
  Hello, {{ user.username }}!
{% else %}
  <a href="{% url 'login' %}">Log in</a>
{% endif %}
  • Trap: Checking request.user != None is wrong — AnonymousUser is not None. Always check request.user.is_authenticated.

lessons.title: 7. Django's built-in auth URLs
lessons.html:
• Django provides ready-made login/logout/password views. Include them with one line in urls.py:
    • from django.contrib.auth import views as auth_views

urlpatterns = [
    path('accounts/', include('django.contrib.auth.urls')),
]
  • This registers: /accounts/login/, /accounts/logout/, /accounts/password_change/, /accounts/password_reset/, and others.
  • You only need to supply the templates. Django looks for them at registration/login.html, registration/logged_out.html, etc.
  • After login, Django redirects to settings.LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL (default: /accounts/profile/). Override it:
    # settings.py
LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL = '/'
LOGIN_URL = '/accounts/login/'
LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL = '/'
  • Trap: If you don't set LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL, Django redirects to /accounts/profile/ which doesn't exist in most projects — giving a 404 after login.

cards.q: What does MVT stand for in Django, and what does each letter do?
cards.ans: Model (database layer, ORM), View (business logic, processes request), Template (HTML presentation layer). urls.py connects URLs to views.
cards.why: Django's MVT maps to MVC: Model=Model, View=Controller, Template=View.

cards.q: How is Django's MVT different from the classic MVC pattern?
cards.ans: In MVC: Model=data, View=presentation, Controller=logic. In Django MVT: Model=data, Template=presentation (MVC View), View=logic (MVC Controller). The naming is swapped for View/Template vs View/Controller.
cards.why: This is a classic Part 2 written question in Tek-up exams.

cards.q: What is the purpose of a virtual environment in Django development?
cards.ans: It creates an isolated Python environment per project so each project can have its own dependency versions without conflicts. E.g. app1 uses Django 4.2, app2 uses Django 5.1 — no clash.
cards.why: Appear in Part 2 as 'explain with example'.

cards.q: What command creates a new Django project named 'mysite'?
cards.ans:
django-admin startproject mysite .
The dot (.) puts files in the current folder. Without it, Django creates a nested mysite/mysite/ structure.

cards.q: Name the files inside a Django project folder and their role.
cards.ans: manage.py = command runner (runserver, migrate, startapp). settings.py = all config. urls.py = main URL router. wsgi.py = WSGI server interface. asgi.py = async server interface. __init__.py = marks it as a package.
cards.why: Exam Q3 tested which files are used for deployment (asgi.py, wsgi.py).

cards.q: What command creates a new app named 'pages' inside a Django project?
cards.ans: python manage.py startapp pages
cards.why: Exam Q4 tested the exact syntax — answer C is correct.

cards.q: After creating an app, what must you do in settings.py?
cards.ans:
Add the app name to INSTALLED_APPS. Example:
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    'pages',  # your new app
]
cards.why: Without this, Django ignores the app. Models won't migrate.

cards.q: What does this view return?
cards.out: An HTTP 200 response with body: Hello word
cards.why: HttpResponse directly returns text/HTML without a template. Verified running Django 5.1.

cards.q: What crash happens if a view function has no return statement?
cards.code:
def broken_view(request):
    x = 1 + 1  # forgot to return
cards.out: ValueError: The view returned None instead of an HttpResponse object.
cards.why: Django checks the return value and raises ValueError if it's None.

cards.q: Show the two-step URL routing pattern: app urls.py + project urls.py.
cards.ans:
App (pages/urls.py):
from django.urls import path
from .views import home_page_view
urlpatterns = [path('home/', home_page_view, name='home')]

Project (urls.py):
from django.urls import path, include
urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('pages/', include('pages.urls')),
]
cards.why: include() delegates all /pages/... URLs to the app's own urlpatterns.

cards.q: What does the name= parameter in path() do?
cards.code: path('home/', home_page_view, name='home')
cards.ans: It gives the URL a name so you can reference it by name instead of hardcoding the path. In templates: {% url 'home' %}. In Python: reverse('home'). If the URL path changes later, only the path() call changes — not every template.
cards.why: Classic Part 2 question: 'Role of the name parameter in routes'.

cards.q: What is the trap with include() — which of these is WRONG?
cards.code:
# A:
path('pages/', include(pages.urls))
# B:
path('pages/', include('pages.urls'))
cards.out: A is wrong. include() takes a string 'pages.urls', not the module object pages.urls.
cards.why: Common student mistake: forgetting the quotes around the dotted path.

cards.q: What is the difference between HttpResponse and render()?
cards.ans:
HttpResponse returns raw content (text, HTML string) directly. render() loads a template file, fills it with context data, and returns an HttpResponse — specifically designed for HTML pages. Example: HttpResponse('

Hello

') vs render(request, 'home.html', {'name': 'Malak'})
cards.why: Exam correction Part 2 explicitly asks this question.

cards.q: Why do we put templates in appname/templates/appname/ (double folder)?
cards.ans: To avoid name clashes. If two apps both have templates/home.html, Django picks one unpredictably. With the double folder, one is website/home.html and the other is meetings/home.html — no clash. Always reference templates with the prefix: render(request, 'website/home.html').
cards.why: A subtle trap that causes bugs in multi-app projects.

cards.q: What does get_object_or_404 do that plain .get() doesn't?
cards.ans: If the object doesn't exist, .get() raises ObjectDoesNotExist and Django shows a 500 error (server crash). get_object_or_404 raises Http404 instead, which shows a proper 404 page — better UX and security (don't expose stack traces to users).

cards.q: Complete this URL pattern to capture an integer id from the URL /meetings/5/
cards.why: <int:id> tells Django: match only integers here, and pass the value to the view as a keyword argument named 'id'.

cards.q: Write the template loop that shows a list of meeting titles as links.
cards.ans:
{% for meeting in meetings %}
  • {{ meeting.title }}
    • {% endfor %}
cards.why: {% url 'detail' meeting.id %} generates /meetings/5/ from the named URL. {{ meeting.title }} displays the field.

cards.q: Show base.html and a child template that extends it.
cards.why: extends must be the very first line. Block names must match exactly between parent and child.

cards.q: What is the trap with {% extends %} in a child template?
cards.ans: {% extends 'base.html' %} MUST be the very first line of the template. Any HTML written before it is silently discarded by Django.
cards.why: Classic beginner mistake: putting a DOCTYPE or comment before extends.

cards.q: What error happens when you use {% static %} without {% load static %}?
cards.code:
<!-- Missing {% load static %} -->
<link href="{% static 'style.css' %}">
cards.out: TemplateSyntaxError: Invalid block tag on line 1: 'static'
cards.why: {% load static %} must appear at the top of any template that uses the {% static %} tag.

cards.q: What is the difference between {% include %} and {% extends %}?
cards.ans:
{% extends 'base.html' %} = inheritance: the child template fills blocks inside the parent layout. Only one base allowed per template.
{% include 'navbar.html' %} = composition: inserts a fragment inline. No block system. Can use multiple includes in one template.

cards.q: Name three important settings in settings.py and explain their role.
cards.ans:
1. INSTALLED_APPS — list of activated apps (built-in + yours). Without it, Django ignores your app.
2. DATABASES — database connection config (engine, name, host, user, password).
3. STATIC_URL — URL prefix for static files. STATIC_ROOT — where collectstatic gathers files for production.
Bonus: TEMPLATES — list of template engines and their settings (DIRS, APP_DIRS).
cards.why: Exam Part 2 Q2 asks exactly this.

cards.q: [Part 2] What is the Django ORM? Why use it instead of raw SQL?
cards.ans: ORM = Object-Relational Mapping. It bridges Python objects and database tables. Models map to tables, attributes map to columns, instances map to rows. Django generates all SQL automatically. Benefits: (1) Write Python instead of SQL. (2) Switch databases without changing your code. (3) Built-in SQL injection protection.
cards.why: Exam Part 2 always asks to explain the ORM. Know the mapping: class=table, attribute=column, instance=row.

cards.q: What is the difference between null=True and blank=True on a model field?
cards.ans:
null=True = database level: allows NULL in the column.
blank=True = form validation level: allows the field to be submitted empty.
They are independent — you can have one, both, or neither.
Rule: for text fields (CharField, TextField) use blank=True only. Using null=True on text fields stores both NULL and '' as 'empty', causing inconsistent queries.
cards.why: Classic exam trap — students confuse null (database) with blank (forms). They test different layers.

cards.q: What are the 3 steps of the migration workflow?
cards.ans:
1. Edit models.py (add, change, or delete a field or model)
2. python manage.py makemigrations   — generates the script
3. python manage.py migrate           — runs the script on the DB

Never skip step 2 or 3. Always in this order.
cards.why: The most common Django mistake: changing a model and forgetting to migrate. Results in OperationalError: no such column.

cards.q: What does each migration command do?
cards.ans:
makemigrations — reads models.py, diffs vs last migration, writes a new script in migrations/
migrate — runs pending scripts, creates/alters DB tables
showmigrations — lists all migrations: [X] applied, [ ] pending
sqlmigrate app 0001 — shows the SQL migrate would run, without running it
cards.why: Exam often asks: 'Which command applies migrations?' Answer: migrate (not makemigrations).

cards.q: What does __str__ do and why does every model need it?
cards.why: Without __str__, Django shows 'Meeting object (1)' everywhere — in admin, print(), templates. Must return a string. Returning an integer raises TypeError.

cards.q: What is the difference between CharField and TextField?
cards.ans:
CharField: short text, REQUIRES max_length=N, stored as VARCHAR.
TextField: long text, no max_length needed, stored as TEXT.
Use CharField for names/titles/codes. Use TextField for descriptions/messages/body text.
cards.why: Forgetting max_length on CharField raises: SystemCheckError: CharField must define max_length.

cards.q: What field type should you use for a price (e.g. 19.99)?
cards.ans:
DecimalField(max_digits=6, decimal_places=2) — exact.
NOT FloatField — floats have rounding errors (19.99 becomes 19.990000001). DecimalField is precise. max_digits = total digits. decimal_places = digits after the dot.
For 999.99: max_digits=5, decimal_places=2.
cards.why: Classic exam question. DecimalField is the correct answer for money/prices.

cards.q: [Part 3 — Ex7] Complete models.py for the Job application system (from real exam).
cards.out:
(1) CharField
(2) TextField
(3) ForeignKey
(4) Job
(5) CASCADE
(6) DateField

Full solution — verified running:
class Job(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    description = models.TextField()
    def __str__(self): return self.title

class Application(models.Model):
    candidate_name = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    job = models.ForeignKey(Job, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    status = models.CharField(max_length=10)
    application_date = models.DateField(auto_now_add=True)
    def __str__(self): return f'{self.candidate_name} - {self.job.title}'
cards.why: (1) CharField needs max_length. (2) TextField for long description. (3) ForeignKey = many-to-one. (4) Job = related model. (5) CASCADE = delete Applications when Job deleted. (6) DateField with auto_now_add sets date on creation automatically.

cards.q: [Part 2] What is Django Admin? What can you do with it?
cards.ans: Django Admin is a built-in web interface for managing your app's data — full CRUD (create, read, update, delete) for any registered model, auto-generated from your models. Access at /admin/ after creating a superuser. Use for: data management during development, back-office tasks for staff, quick debugging. NOT for end-users.
cards.why: Exam Part 2 often asks to describe the admin or explain the two parts of a web app (front-end for users, admin for staff).

cards.q: What is the minimum code to make Meeting appear in the Admin?

# meetings/admin.py

from .models import Meeting

admin.site.register(Meeting)
cards.out:
Meeting appears at /admin/meetings/meeting/
Verified: admin.site.is_registered(Meeting) = True
cards.why: admin.site.register(Model) is all you need. Without it, the model is invisible in admin — no error, just silently missing.

cards.q: What is the correct order to get the Admin panel working on a fresh project?
cards.ans:
1. python manage.py migrate        (creates auth_user table)
2. python manage.py createsuperuser (creates admin account)
3. Register models in admin.py
4. python manage.py runserver
5. Visit http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/

Trap: running createsuperuser before migrate gives 'no such table: auth_user'.
cards.why: The order matters. migrate must come first. This is a classic exam procedure question.

admin.site.register(Meeting)

Verified: admin.site.is_registered(Meeting) = True, admin.site.is_registered(Room) = True
cards.why: Import admin from django.contrib. Import models with relative import (.models). register() takes the model class — not a string.

cards.q: [Part 2] What are the three Django relation field types and when do you use each?
cards.ans:
ForeignKey — one-to-many: many Meetings → one Room. Defined on the 'many' side.
OneToOneField — one-to-one: one User → one Profile. Each object linked to exactly one other.
ManyToManyField — many-to-many: many Students ↔ many Courses. Django creates a join table automatically.
cards.why: Exam Part 2 and Part 3 test knowing which field type to use. ForeignKey appears in every exam problem.

cards.q: What does on_delete=models.CASCADE do?
cards.ans:
When the parent object is deleted, all related child objects are also deleted automatically.
Example: Room deleted → all Meetings in that Room are deleted.
Verified: r.delete() → Meeting.objects.get(pk=m.pk) raises DoesNotExist.
cards.why: on_delete is required on ForeignKey. CASCADE is the most common choice and appears in every exam models.py completion.

cards.q: What is the difference between on_delete=CASCADE, SET_NULL and PROTECT?
cards.ans:
CASCADE — delete all children when parent is deleted. Most common.
SET_NULL — set FK to NULL when parent deleted. Requires null=True on the field. Child objects are kept.
PROTECT — prevent deletion of parent if any children exist. Raises ProtectedError.
cards.why: Exam MCQ tests which on_delete option to use in a given scenario.

cards.q: Show ForeignKey — forward and reverse access.
cards.code:
# Forward: meeting → room
m = Meeting.objects.get(pk=1)
print(m.room.name)        # forward FK

# Reverse: room → all its meetings
r = Room.objects.get(pk=1)
print(r.meeting_set.all())  # reverse accessor
cards.out:
m.room.name     → 'Conf A'
r.meeting_set.all() → QuerySet of all Meetings in that room

Verified: FK forward='Conf A', FK reverse count >= 2
cards.why: Forward access uses the field name. Reverse uses modelname_set by default, or the related_name you defined.

cards.q: What does related_name do on a ForeignKey?
cards.code:
class Meeting(models.Model):
    room = models.ForeignKey(Room,
        on_delete=models.CASCADE,
        related_name='meetings')
cards.out:
Without related_name: room.meeting_set.all()
With related_name='meetings': room.meetings.all()

Same data, different accessor name.
cards.why: related_name is also required when a model has two FKs to the same model — without it Django raises an accessor name clash error.

Result: job.applications.all() returns all applications for that job.

cards.q: [Part 2] What is the role of {% csrf_token %} in a Django form?
cards.ans: It generates a hidden input with a secret token that Django verifies on form submission. This protects against CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) attacks — where a malicious site tricks a logged-in user into submitting a form on your site. Without it, Django returns 403 Forbidden on POST. This was question 1 on the actual exam.
cards.why: Exam Q1 tested exactly this. Answer: {% csrf_token %}.

cards.q: What is the difference between {% extends %} and {% include %}?
cards.ans:
{% extends 'base.html' %} = template inheritance. The child fills named blocks in the base layout. Must be the first line. Only one base per template.
{% include 'navbar.html' %} = composition. Inserts a template fragment inline. No block system. Can use multiple includes.
cards.why: Classic confusion point. Inheritance = one base, fill holes. Include = paste a snippet.

cards.q: What is the correct template syntax for each of these?
cards.why: Exam Part 3 Q4 always asks to complete a template. Know all these tags by heart.

cards.q: [Part 3 — Ex13] Complete this template to list jobs with a fallback message.

{% _____(1)_____ "base.html" %} {% block content %}

Job List

    _____(2)_____ job in jobs _____
  • {{ job._____(3)_____ }}
    • _____(4)_____
  • No jobs available.
    • _____(5)_____
{% endblock %}
cards.why: Exact pattern from exam Part 3 Q4 (Job/Application exam). extends must be line 1. {% empty %} handles zero items.

cards.q: [Part 3 — Ex14] Complete this template for a job_list CBV (from exam).

(2) jobs  (the context_object_name from JobListView)
(3) job.title
(4) job.description
