Note: context_object_name='jobs' in the CBV means the template variable is 'jobs'.
Verified: this is exactly the exam question.
cards.why: When using ListView with context_object_name='jobs', the template loop uses 'jobs'. If context_object_name is not set, it defaults to 'job_list'.

cards.q: What is the most useful forloop variable inside {% for %}?
cards.why: forloop.counter = 1-based position. forloop.counter0 = 0-based. forloop.first = True on first iteration. forloop.last = True on last. These are available inside any {% for %} block.

cards.q: What are the three methods for handling forms in Django?
cards.why: Method 1: raw request.POST — read values directly, no validation class. Method 2: forms.Form — define a form class, use is_valid() and cleaned_data. Method 3: forms.ModelForm — auto-generates fields from a model, form.save() writes to the DB.

cards.q: What does request.POST['firstname'] do, and what is the safer alternative?
cards.code: firstname = request.POST['firstname']
cards.why: request.POST is a dict-like object. ['firstname'] raises KeyError if the field is absent. The safer alternative is request.POST.get('firstname', '') which returns a default if the key is missing.

cards.q: Complete the view: bind the form to POST data, validate, then save.
cards.why: request.POST or None: on GET the form is unbound (None), on POST it is bound to the submitted data. is_valid() runs validators. cleaned_data is a dict of validated Python values.

cards.q: Write the ModelForm for a Contact model with fields firstname, lastname, email, message.
cards.why: ModelForm requires an inner Meta class with model= and fields=. fields can be a list of field names or '__all__'. The form generates input widgets from the model field types automatically.

cards.q: What is the one-line difference between a forms.Form view and a forms.ModelForm view?
cards.why: With forms.Form you must write the save logic yourself: Contact.objects.create(**form.cleaned_data). With forms.ModelForm you just call form.save() and it creates the row for you.

cards.q: What does {{ form.as_p }} render, and what tag must appear before it in the template?
cards.code:
<form method="post">
  ___(1)___
  {{ form.___(2)___ }}
  <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>
cards.why:
{% csrf_token %} generates a hidden input with a security token. Without it Django returns 403 Forbidden. form.as_p wraps each field in

tags — the simplest way to render a form.

cards.q: Write a clean_date method that rejects past dates.
cards.why: clean_<field> runs after the field's built-in validation. It must raise ValidationError for invalid data, or return the value for valid data. Forgetting the return makes cleaned_data['date'] become None.

cards.q: What is a widget, and how do you change a CharField to render as a Textarea?
cards.code:
class ContactForm(forms.Form):
    msg = forms.CharField(widget=___(1)___)
cards.why: A widget controls the HTML input element rendered for a field. CharField defaults to TextInput (single line). Passing widget=forms.Textarea makes it a multi-line <textarea> instead.

cards.q: When is it wrong to access form.cleaned_data?
cards.code:
form = ContactForm(request.POST)
# BUG: accessing cleaned_data before is_valid()
name = form.cleaned_data['firstname']
cards.why: cleaned_data is populated only after is_valid() is called. Accessing it before raises AttributeError: 'ContactForm' object has no attribute 'cleaned_data'. Always call is_valid() first and check it returns True.

cards.q: What HTTP method must the HTML <form> tag use for POST data, and why?
cards.code:
<form ___(1)___="post">
  {% csrf_token %}
  ...
</form>
cards.why: Without method="post", the browser defaults to GET. GET sends data in the URL query string (visible, no body). request.POST will be empty and the view logic won't run. POST sends data in the request body, which is required for creates/updates.

cards.q: What is a QuerySet, and when does it hit the database?
cards.why: A QuerySet is a lazy collection of model instances. It is built up in Python without touching the database. The SQL query runs only when you evaluate the QuerySet: iterate over it, convert to list, call len(), use a boolean check, or slice it.

cards.q: What is the difference between filter() and get()?
cards.code:
# A
rooms = Room.objects.filter(floor=1)
# B
room  = Room.objects.get(pk=1)
cards.why: filter() always returns a QuerySet (possibly empty). get() returns exactly one object — it raises DoesNotExist if nothing matches, and MultipleObjectsReturned if more than one matches. Use get() only when you are certain exactly one row exists.

cards.q: Write a query for all meetings whose title contains 'Django' (case-insensitive).
cards.code: meetings = Meeting.objects.filter(___(1)___='django')
cards.why: Field lookups use double underscores: field__lookup=value. __icontains maps to SQL LIKE '%django%' with no case sensitivity. __contains is case-sensitive.

cards.q: Get the first 5 rooms ordered by name descending.
cards.code: rooms = Room.objects.order_by(___(1)___)___(2)___
cards.why: order_by('-name') sorts Z→A (descending prefix is -). [:5] is Python slice syntax which Django translates to SQL LIMIT 5.

cards.q: Create a Room and then update its name. Show both save styles.
cards.code:
# create
r = Room.objects.___(1)___(name='Lab', floor=2, room_number=201)

# update
r.___(2)___ = 'Main Lab'
r.___(3)___()
cards.why: objects.create() is shorthand for Room(...).save(). To update, modify the attribute then call .save() — this runs UPDATE WHERE pk=... on the database.

cards.q: Delete all rooms on floor 99 in a single database query.
cards.why: filter().delete() issues a single DELETE FROM WHERE SQL statement. It's faster than fetching each row and calling .delete() individually, but it bypasses model delete() signals.

cards.q: What does .values('name', 'floor') return instead of a normal QuerySet?
cards.code:
result = Room.objects.values('name', 'floor')[:2]
# result = ___
cards.why: .values() returns a QuerySet of dicts, not model instances. Each dict contains only the requested fields. This is lighter than loading full objects when you only need a few columns.

cards.q: What problem does select_related() solve, and when should you use it?
cards.why: Without select_related, accessing m.room triggers a new SQL query for every meeting row (N+1 problem). select_related('room') fetches meetings and rooms in a single JOIN query.

cards.q: What is Room.DoesNotExist and when is it raised?
cards.why: Every Django model gets a DoesNotExist exception class automatically. It is raised by .get() when no row matches the lookup. It's a subclass of ObjectDoesNotExist. Catch it as Room.DoesNotExist, not a generic Exception.

cards.q: Rewrite this crash-prone view to return a 404 instead of a 500.
cards.why: get_object_or_404(Room, pk=pk) calls .get() internally and catches DoesNotExist, raising Http404 instead, which Django renders as a proper 404 page rather than a 500 server error.

cards.q: How do you wire a CBV into urls.py?
cards.code: path('posts/', PostListView.___(1)___, name='post-list')
cards.why: CBVs are classes, not callables. .as_view() returns a function that Django can call. Forgetting it passes the class itself and raises TypeError at runtime.

cards.q: Write a ListView for BlogPost with context_object_name='posts'.
cards.code:
from django.views.generic import ___(1)___

class PostListView(___(1)___):
    model = ___(2)___
    template_name = 'blog/post_list.html'
    context_object_name = ___(3)___
cards.why: ListView fetches all rows of model and puts them in context. context_object_name='posts' means the template uses {% for post in posts %}. Without it the default key is 'blogpost_list'.

cards.q: Override get_queryset() to show only the current user's posts, newest first.
cards.why: get_queryset() is the correct hook for dynamic queries. self.request.user is the logged-in user. '-created_on' sorts descending (newest first). Never use a class-level queryset= for dynamic filtering.

cards.q: What URL pattern does DetailView require, and what does it use to look up the object?
cards.code: path('posts/<___(1)___:___(2)___/', PostDetailView.as_view(), name='post-detail')
cards.why: DetailView uses pk (primary key) from the URL by default. The URL converter int: restricts it to integers. If you use a different kwarg name like id, set pk_url_kwarg = 'id' on the view.

cards.q: Write a CreateView for BlogPost. What must success_url use instead of reverse()?
cards.code:
from django.urls import ___(1)___

class PostCreateView(CreateView):
    model = BlogPost
    fields = ['title', 'content', 'author']
    success_url = ___(1)___('post-list')
cards.why: reverse_lazy() is evaluated when first accessed, not at class definition time. reverse() runs immediately at import — before urls.py is fully loaded — causing NoReverseMatch.

cards.q: What is the difference between CreateView and UpdateView?
cards.why: CreateView starts with an empty form and INSERT on POST. UpdateView loads an existing object by pk, pre-fills the form with its current data, and UPDATE on POST. They share the same template name convention (<model>_form.html).

cards.q: What HTTP method triggers the actual deletion in DeleteView, and what does GET do?
cards.why: GET shows the confirmation template (_confirm_delete.html). POST triggers the deletion. This two-step design prevents accidental or CSRF-triggered deletes from a simple link click.

cards.q: Add login protection to a CreateView using the correct mixin.
cards.code:
from django.contrib.auth.mixins import ___(1)___

class PostCreateView(___(1)___, CreateView):
    model = BlogPost
    fields = ['title', 'content']
    success_url = reverse_lazy('post-list')
cards.why: LoginRequiredMixin must be listed first (before CreateView) so its dispatch() runs before the view logic. Anonymous users are redirected to LOGIN_URL. For FBVs use @login_required instead.

cards.q: What is the default context name and default template name for a ListView on BlogPost?
cards.why: Django derives both from the model name in lowercase. Set context_object_name and template_name explicitly to use cleaner names and avoid being tied to the model name.

cards.q: What are the five generic CBVs and their purpose in one word each?
cards.out:
ListView     — list all rows
DetailView   — show one row
CreateView   — new row form
UpdateView   — edit existing row
DeleteView   — confirm + delete
cards.why: These five cover the full CRUD cycle: Create (CreateView), Read (ListView + DetailView), Update (UpdateView), Delete (DeleteView). They all live in django.views.generic.

cards.q: Create a user safely. What is wrong with the second version?
cards.code:
# CORRECT
u = User.objects.create_user(
    username='malak', password='secret123')

# BUG
u = User.objects.create(
    username='malak', password='secret123')
cards.out:
Bug: .create() stores password as plain text.
create_user() hashes the password with PBKDF2.
cards.why: Django uses PBKDF2 (or Argon2/bcrypt if configured) to hash passwords. create_user() calls set_password() internally. .create() bypasses this and stores the raw string — anyone who reads the DB can see the password.

cards.q: Complete the login view.
cards.why: authenticate() checks the credentials and returns the User or None. login() creates the session. The order is mandatory — authenticate first, then login.

cards.q: Write the logout view.
cards.why: logout(request) flushes the session data and sets request.user to AnonymousUser. After this call the user is no longer authenticated. The view should only accept POST requests to prevent CSRF logout via a link.

cards.q: Use UserCreationForm to build a signup view that logs the user in immediately.
cards.why: UserCreationForm is Django's built-in form for user registration. form.save() hashes the password and creates the User. login() then creates a session so the user is immediately authenticated.

cards.q: What is wrong with this CBV protection?
cards.why: @login_required is a decorator for functions. Applying it to a class does nothing useful. For CBVs, use LoginRequiredMixin as the first base class — its dispatch() method runs before the view and redirects anonymous users.

cards.q: Show the template snippet that greets logged-in users and shows a login link to others.
cards.why: user is available in every template via the auth context processor (enabled by default). is_authenticated is True for logged-in users, False for AnonymousUser. Never check user != None — AnonymousUser is not None.

cards.q: What three settings control redirect URLs for auth views?
cards.why: LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL: where to go after a successful login (default: /accounts/profile/). LOGIN_URL: where @login_required sends anonymous users (default: /accounts/login/). LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL: where to go after logout.

cards.q: What is the difference between is_staff, is_superuser, and is_active?
cards.out:
is_active=False   → account disabled, cannot log in
is_staff=True     → can access /admin/ panel
is_superuser=True → all permissions, bypasses all checks
cards.why: is_active controls whether the account exists functionally. is_staff grants admin panel access. is_superuser is the highest privilege level — it overrides all permission checks. A new user gets is_active=True, is_staff=False, is_superuser=False.

cards.q: What does authenticate() return when credentials are wrong?
cards.code:
user = authenticate(username='malak', password='wrong')
print(user)  # prints: ___
cards.why: authenticate() returns None if credentials don't match any user. Always check 'if user is not None' before calling login(). Calling login(request, None) raises AttributeError.

cards.q: Include Django's built-in auth URLs in one line. What routes does it add?
cards.code: path('accounts/', include(___(1)___))
cards.why: django.contrib.auth.urls is a pre-built URL conf. It wires all the auth views. You only need to provide the templates (registration/login.html etc.). Set LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL in settings.py or it redirects to /accounts/profile/ (404 by default).

mcq.q: Which command correctly creates a Django application named 'blog'?
mcq.why: python manage.py startapp blog is correct. django-admin is for projects (startproject), not apps. newapp and createapp do not exist — they are made-up commands. This was question 4 on the actual exam.

mcq.q: In Django's MVT pattern, which component handles the business logic and processes HTTP requests?
mcq.why: The View in Django = the Controller in MVC. It receives the HTTP request, runs logic (queries, calculations), and returns a response. The Template handles presentation. The Model handles data. 'Controller' is the MVC name — Django doesn't use that term.

mcq.q: In Django, what is the Template equivalent in classic MVC architecture?
mcq.why: Django Template = MVC View (presentation layer). Django View = MVC Controller (logic layer). The names are swapped — the most common confusion in exams.

mcq.q: Which files are used by default for server deployment in Django? (Choose 2)
mcq.why: wsgi.py = WSGI server interface (Gunicorn, uWSGI, Apache). asgi.py = ASGI server interface (Daphne, Uvicorn — for async/WebSocket). manage.py is for local dev commands. This was exam Q3.

mcq.q: How do you correctly include an app's URLs in the project's urls.py?
mcq.code:
# Which is correct?
# A:
path('blog/', include('blog.urls'))
# B:
path('blog/', include(blog.urls))
# C:
path('blog/urls', blog)
# D:
path('route', my_view)
mcq.why: include() takes a string: 'blog.urls'. Passing the module object blog.urls without quotes raises a NameError (unless you imported it). This was exam Q10.

mcq.q: A URL pattern path('articles/<int:id>/', views.detail) is defined. Which URL will it match?
mcq.why: <int:id> matches only positive integers. hello is a string → no match. Missing the number → no match. 3.5 is a float, not an integer → no match.

mcq.q: What is wrong with this view?
mcq.ok: It returns None — Django will raise ValueError
bad: x = 2 + 2 is a syntax error in Django
mcq.why: Every Django view must return an HttpResponse (or subclass). This function returns None implicitly. Django checks the return value and raises ValueError: The view returned None instead of an HttpResponse object.

mcq.q: What does render() return?
mcq.ok: An HttpResponse containing the rendered HTML of home.html with name='Malak' substituted
bad: A string containing the HTML source
A dict with the context data
mcq.why: render() is a shortcut that loads the template, substitutes the context variables, and returns a full HttpResponse object (status 200, Content-Type text/html). It is not a string or a dict.

mcq.q: You create a new app 'shop' but its models are never found by migrate. What is the most likely cause?
mcq.ok: 'shop' is not in INSTALLED_APPS in settings.py
bad: You need to run startapp again
Django only supports one app per project
mcq.why: Django only processes apps that are listed in INSTALLED_APPS. If 'shop' is not there, Django ignores its models.py entirely — no migration files will be created.

mcq.q: What is the correct syntax to display a template variable in Django?
mcq.why: Django uses {{ variable }} for output and {% tag %} for logic. <%= %> is ERB (Ruby). <% %> is ASP/JSP. This was in the exam correction.

mcq.q: What is the correct way to comment a block in a Django template?
bad: {# single line only works for blocks #}
mcq.why: {% comment %}...{% endcomment %} for multi-line blocks. {# ... #} for single-line comments. HTML comments <!-- --> are NOT Django comments — the template engine still evaluates them. This was exam Q12.

mcq.q: What can a Django template NOT do?
mcq.why: Templates handle presentation only. Database access happens in the View (which queries the Model and passes results as context). Templates cannot import Python modules or run ORM queries. This was exam Q7.

mcq.q: Given this urls.py, what URL resolves for {% url 'home' %}?
mcq.code:
urlpatterns = [
    path('pages/', include('pages.urls')),
]
# pages/urls.py:
urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.home_view, name='home'),
]
mcq.why: The project routes /pages/ to the pages app. Inside the app, path('') matches the root of that prefix — so the full URL is /pages/. name='home' resolves to that combined path.

mcq.q: What is the difference between these two views?
mcq.ok: View A returns a plain string; View B loads and renders an HTML template file
bad: View A is for GET, View B is for POST
View B returns JSON, View A returns HTML
mcq.why: HttpResponse takes content directly (string, bytes). render() loads a template file from disk, substitutes context variables, and returns an HttpResponse. For real pages you almost always use render().

mcq.q: What does get_object_or_404(Meeting, pk=5) do if no Meeting with pk=5 exists?
mcq.ok: Raises Http404, Django returns a 404 page
bad: Raises Meeting.DoesNotExist and shows a 500 error
Creates a new Meeting with pk=5
mcq.why: get_object_or_404 catches DoesNotExist and re-raises it as Http404 — resulting in a proper 404 response. Plain .get() raises DoesNotExist which Django turns into a 500 server error (ugly and insecure).

mcq.q: What is the trap in this child template?
mcq.ok: {% extends %} must be the FIRST line — the DOCTYPE before it is silently ignored
bad: DOCTYPE is not allowed in Django templates
{% block content %} needs an id attribute
mcq.why: Django requires {% extends %} to be the very first token in the template. Anything before it (even whitespace or DOCTYPE) is silently discarded. The whole page will render without the DOCTYPE.

mcq.q: Which field type is correct for a product price like 19.99?
mcq.why: DecimalField is exact — 19.99 stays 19.99. FloatField has rounding errors (19.99 may become 19.990000001). IntegerField can't store decimals. CharField stores text.

mcq.q: What happens if you define a CharField without max_length?
mcq.ok: Django raises a system check error: CharField must define max_length
bad: It works fine with unlimited length
mcq.why: max_length is required for CharField. Django system checks catch this before the server starts. Use TextField() if you need unlimited length.

mcq.q: You added a new field to a model. Which command creates the migration script?
mcq.why: makemigrations generates the migration script. migrate applies it. startmigration and createmigration do not exist. Remember: make first, then migrate.

mcq.q: Which command applies pending migrations to the database?
mcq.why: migrate applies the scripts to the actual database. makemigrations only generates the scripts. runmigrations and applymigrations do not exist. Tested in the exam correction.

mcq.q: What does python manage.py showmigrations display?
mcq.ok: A list of all migrations with [X] for applied and [ ] for pending
bad: Only the SQL that will be run
mcq.why: showmigrations lists ALL migrations for every app. [X] = applied, [ ] = pending. sqlmigrate shows SQL for a specific migration.

mcq.q: What does python manage.py sqlmigrate meetings 0001 do?
mcq.ok: Prints the SQL for migration 0001 without running it
mcq.why: sqlmigrate is a read-only inspection tool. It shows the SQL Django would generate — without modifying the database. Useful for understanding and debugging schema changes.

mcq.q: What is the difference between null=True and blank=True?
mcq.ok: null=True allows NULL in the database; blank=True allows empty value in forms
bad: They are identical — both make the field optional
null=True is for forms; blank=True is for the database
mcq.why: null=True = database-level (column can store NULL). blank=True = form-validation-level (field can be submitted empty). Independent settings. For text fields, prefer blank=True without null=True.

mcq.q: What does __str__ on a model control?
mcq.ok: How the object is displayed as text — in admin, print(), and templates
bad: It is the primary key of the model
It is called automatically when the model is saved
It defines a string column in the database
mcq.why: Without __str__: Room object (1). With it: Salle A: room 201. Called whenever Python needs a string: print(), admin list view, {{ room }} in templates. Verified output: Salle A: room 201 on floor 2.

mcq.q: You edit models.py but don't run any management commands. What happens when you query the new field?
mcq.code:
# Added location to Meeting — no makemigrations/migrate
Meeting.objects.filter(location='Room 101')
bad: Django auto-detects the change and updates the table
mcq.why: Editing models.py does NOT change the database. You must run makemigrations then migrate. Without them, the column doesn't exist. This is the most common Django beginner mistake.

mcq.q: Which field stores a date AND time (e.g. '2027-01-15 09:30:00')?
mcq.why: DateField = date only. TimeField = time only. DateTimeField = both. DateAndTimeField does not exist in Django.

mcq.q: What does auto_now_add=True do on a DateField?
mcq.ok: Sets the date to today when the object is created; cannot be changed later
bad: Sets the date to today every time the object is saved
Makes the field optional with default=today
mcq.why: auto_now_add=True = set once at creation, then read-only. auto_now=True = update on every save. With auto_now_add, the field is excluded from forms — you cannot set it manually.

mcq.q: In which order must you run commands after adding a field to a model?
mcq.why: makemigrations generates the script. migrate runs it. Both are required, always in this order. Running migrate first when no script exists does nothing. Skipping migrate means the database is never updated.

mcq.q: What is the generated database table name for this model?
mcq.why: Django generates table names as appname_modelname, all lowercase. App meetings + model Room = table meetings_room. Verified via sqlmigrate: CREATE TABLE "meetings_room".

mcq.q: In Django ORM: class / attribute / instance maps to what in the database?
mcq.why: Class = table definition. Attribute = column. Instance (object) = row. This is the core ORM mapping — appears in exam Part 2 written answers.

mcq.q: Which field would you use for a user biography (long text, no fixed limit)?
mcq.why: TextField() is designed for unlimited-length text — stored as TEXT in the database. CharField requires max_length and is VARCHAR. LongTextField does not exist in Django.

mcq.q: What is wrong with this __str__ method?
mcq.code:
def __str__(self):
    return self.duration  # duration is IntegerField
mcq.ok: TypeError — __str__ must return a string, not an integer
mcq.why: __str__ must return a string. self.duration is an integer. Fix: return str(self.duration) or return f"{self.title} ({self.duration}h)".

mcq.q: What is the minimum code to make a model appear in the Django Admin?
mcq.why: admin.site.register(MyModel) in admin.py is all you need. INSTALLED_APPS needs 'django.contrib.admin' (already there by default) but not the model. ModelAdmin is optional — it only customises the display.

mcq.q: What is the correct method to register a model in the admin?
mcq.why: The correct method is admin.site.register(MyModel). admin.register(MyModel) without site doesn't exist as a standalone function. This was explicitly in the exam correction Part 1.

mcq.q: You run createsuperuser but get 'no such table: auth_user'. What did you forget?
mcq.why: createsuperuser needs the auth_user table, which is created by migrate. Always run migrate before createsuperuser. django.contrib.auth is in INSTALLED_APPS by default.

mcq.q: Without __str__ on a model, how are objects shown in the Admin list view?
bad: By their first field value automatically
mcq.why: Without __str__, Python uses the default: ClassName object (pk). The admin displays this literally — useless for humans. Always define __str__ on every model.

mcq.q: What does @admin.register(Meeting) do?
mcq.ok: Registers Meeting with MeetingAdmin — equivalent to admin.site.register(Meeting, MeetingAdmin)
bad: Creates a new Meeting model in the admin database
It is invalid syntax in Django
mcq.why: @admin.register(Model) is a decorator shortcut. Equivalent to admin.site.register(Meeting, MeetingAdmin) — just more concise.

mcq.q: Which field type do you use when many Applications belong to one Job?
mcq.why: Many-to-one relationship = ForeignKey. OneToOneField is for exactly one-to-one. ManyToManyField is for many-to-many. IntegerField stores numbers, not relationships.

mcq.q: What does on_delete=models.CASCADE do when a Room is deleted?
mcq.ok: All Meetings linked to that Room are automatically deleted
bad: The room field on Meetings is set to NULL
Django raises an error and prevents deletion
Meetings are kept and their room field is left unchanged
mcq.why: CASCADE propagates the delete to all children. Room deleted → all its Meetings deleted. Use SET_NULL (with null=True) to keep Meetings but clear their room field. Verified: Meeting.objects.get(pk=m.pk) raises DoesNotExist after room is deleted.

mcq.q: You want to delete a Room only if it has no Meetings. Which on_delete option do you use?
mcq.why: PROTECT raises ProtectedError when you try to delete a parent that still has children. This prevents accidental data loss. CASCADE would delete the children. SET_NULL would orphan them.

mcq.q: How do you access all Meetings for a given Room (reverse FK access)?
mcq.why: Django automatically creates a reverse accessor named modelname_set. For Room→Meeting: r.meeting_set.all(). You can rename it with related_name='meetings' → then r.meetings.all(). Meeting.objects.filter(room=r) also works but uses lowercase room.

mcq.q: What is required when you use on_delete=models.SET_NULL?
mcq.ok: null=True must also be set on the field
bad: The Room model must have a nullable primary key
mcq.why: If the FK is set to NULL, the database column must allow NULL. SET_NULL without null=True causes an IntegrityError. Fix: room = models.ForeignKey(Room, on_delete=models.SET_NULL, null=True).

mcq.q: Which relation type does Django use for the User ↔ Profile relationship (one user = one profile)?
mcq.why: OneToOneField enforces that each User has at most one Profile. ForeignKey would allow many Profiles per User. ManyToManyField is for many-to-many. PrimaryKeyField doesn't exist.

mcq.q: What does Django automatically create for a ManyToManyField?
mcq.ok: An intermediate join table (e.g. student_courses) in the database
bad: A new column in the Student table
A new column in the Course table
Nothing — you must create the join table manually
mcq.why: Django automatically creates a join table (e.g. appname_student_courses) with two foreign key columns — one for Student, one for Course. You never define this table yourself.

mcq.q: In which file do you define a ForeignKey relationship between two models?
mcq.ok: models.py — on the model that is on the 'many' side
mcq.why: Relations are defined in models.py. The ForeignKey is placed on the many side — the model that belongs to another. Example: Application has FK to Job (many Applications → one Job).

mcq.q: What does on_delete=models.CASCADE mean in this model?
mcq.ok: If a Job is deleted, all its Applications are deleted too
bad: If an Application is deleted, its Job is deleted too
Jobs cannot be deleted while Applications exist
mcq.why: CASCADE applies to the parent being deleted. Here Job is the parent. Deleting a Job cascades down to its Applications. The Application itself can still be deleted independently.

mcq.q: What is the reverse accessor name for this relationship?
mcq.why: Default reverse accessor = modelname_set (all lowercase). Model BookPost → accessor bookpost_set. Set related_name='posts' to get author.posts.all() instead. Note: filter(Author=author) uses uppercase — wrong. Use filter(author=author).

mcq.q: Which template tag protects a form against CSRF attacks?
mcq.why: {% csrf_token %} generates a hidden input with a secret token. Django checks this token on every POST. Without it: 403 Forbidden. This was question 1 on the actual exam.

mcq.q: What is the correct syntax to display a template variable?
mcq.why: Django uses {{ }} for output and {% %} for logic. <%= %> is ERB (Ruby). <% %> is PHP/ASP. {% variable %} would try to execute 'variable' as a tag — which doesn't exist.

mcq.q: What happens when you use {% static 'style.css' %} without {% load static %}?
bad: Django uses a default static path
mcq.why: {% load static %} must appear before any {% static %} use. Without it, Django doesn't know the static tag and raises TemplateSyntaxError. Verified output: /static/style.css when loaded correctly.

mcq.q: What does {% empty %} do inside a {% for %} loop?
mcq.ok: Renders the empty block when the list has zero items
bad: Clears the list before the loop
Raises an error if the list is empty
mcq.why: {% empty %} is a convenience shortcut inside {% for %}. When the iterable is empty, Django renders the {% empty %} block instead of the loop body. Verified: {% for %}{% empty %}{% endfor %} with [] → 'Nothing here.'

mcq.q: Which Django template filter shows 'N/A' when a variable is empty or missing?
mcq.why: {{ value|default:'N/A' }} returns the default string when value is falsy (empty string, None, 0, []). fallback, or, and empty are not Django filters.

mcq.q: What is the correct way to comment a block of template code?
bad: {# single line only works for blocks #}
mcq.why: {% comment %}...{% endcomment %} for multi-line. {# ... #} for single-line. HTML comments <!-- --> are NOT Django comments — the template engine still evaluates them. This was exam Q12.

mcq.q: What must be true about {% extends %} in a child template?
mcq.ok: It must be the very first line of the template
bad: It can appear anywhere before the first {% block %}
It must be inside a {% block %}
It is optional — you can use {% include %} instead
mcq.why: {% extends %} must be the first token in the template. Any content before it (even whitespace or DOCTYPE) is silently discarded. The whole inheritance mechanism depends on this.

mcq.q: What does {% url 'detail' meeting.id %} generate?
bad: It raises NoReverseMatch if meeting.id is not in the URL
mcq.why: {% url 'name' arg %} calls Django's reverse() to build the URL from the named pattern. It generates /meetings/5/. If the name doesn't exist → NoReverseMatch. Verified: reverse('detail', args=[5]) → /meetings/5/.

mcq.q: What does form.is_valid() do?
mcq.ok: Runs all field validators and populates form.cleaned_data if everything passes
bad: Saves the form data to the database
Returns the raw POST data as a dict
mcq.why: is_valid() triggers validation on every field. If all fields pass, it returns True and sets form.cleaned_data. It never touches the database — that is form.save() (ModelForm only).

mcq.q: You submit a POST form and get HTTP 403 Forbidden. What is the most likely cause?
bad: Missing method="post" on the form tag
The view is not decorated with @login_required
mcq.why: Django's CSRF middleware rejects POST requests that don't carry a matching CSRF token. Adding {% csrf_token %} inside the <form> tag generates a hidden input that satisfies the middleware.

mcq.q: What is the difference between forms.Form and forms.ModelForm?
mcq.ok: ModelForm auto-generates fields from a model and provides form.save() to write to the DB; forms.Form requires manual field definitions and manual save logic
bad: forms.Form supports validation, ModelForm does not
ModelForm cannot render with as_p(); forms.Form can
They are identical — ModelForm is just an alias for forms.Form
mcq.why: ModelForm reads the model's field definitions and creates matching form fields automatically. It also provides .save() which handles both INSERT and UPDATE. forms.Form has no model — you define all fields manually and write your own save logic.

mcq.q: When is form.cleaned_data populated?
mcq.code:
form = ContactForm(request.POST)
# at this point, is cleaned_data available?
mcq.ok: Only after form.is_valid() is called and returns True
bad: As soon as the form is instantiated with POST data
mcq.why: cleaned_data does not exist until is_valid() runs. Accessing it before is_valid() raises AttributeError. After is_valid() returns True, cleaned_data contains validated, converted Python values.

mcq.q:
Which render helper wraps each field in

tags?
mcq.why:
form.as_p() wraps each field in

tags. form.as_table() uses tags (needs outer ). form.as_ul() uses
  • tags (needs outer
      ). as_div() does not exist in standard Django.

mcq.q: You define clean_date() but forget the return statement. What happens?
mcq.ok: cleaned_data['date'] becomes None, silently breaking downstream code
bad: Django raises a RuntimeError about missing return
Nothing — Django uses the original value from request.POST
mcq.why: Python functions that fall off the end return None. cleaned_data['date'] will be None after is_valid(), which looks like a valid result. This is a silent bug — no exception is raised.

mcq.q: What does ContactModelForm(request.POST or None) pass as the first argument on a GET request?
mcq.ok: None — the form is unbound (no data), so it renders empty without validation errors
mcq.why: On a GET request, request.POST is an empty QueryDict which is falsy. 'request.POST or None' evaluates to None. Passing None to a form creates an unbound form — it renders with blank fields and won't validate.

mcq.q: Which widget turns a CharField into a multi-line textarea?
mcq.why: The correct widget class is forms.Textarea (capital T, lowercase area). There is no TextArea, MultilineInput, or LargeTextInput in Django's forms module.

mcq.q: In a ModelForm, what does fields = '__all__' mean?
mcq.ok: Include every field from the model in the form
bad: Exclude all fields — the form will be empty
Use only fields that have blank=True on the model
It is a syntax error — fields must be a list
mcq.why: '__all__' is a special string that tells ModelForm to include every field defined on the model. It is valid syntax. Using it in production is risky because new model fields are automatically included in the form.

mcq.q: What is the purpose of the name attribute on an HTML input?
mcq.ok: It becomes the key in request.POST — e.g. request.POST['firstname']
bad: It is used as the HTML id for CSS styling
It sets the default value of the input
It is required for {% csrf_token %} to work
mcq.why: The browser sends form data as key=value pairs. The name attribute is the key. Without it, the field value is never submitted. request.POST['firstname'] only works if the input has name='firstname'.

mcq.q: When does a QuerySet actually query the database?
mcq.ok: When the QuerySet is evaluated — iterated, sliced, converted to list, or used in a boolean test
mcq.why: QuerySets are lazy. filter() and order_by() just build a query description. The SQL runs only when Python needs the actual data: iterating with for, calling list(), len(), bool(), or slicing.

mcq.q: Room.objects.get(pk=99999) raises which exception?
mcq.why: Every model has a DoesNotExist exception automatically. get() raises it when no matching row is found. Http404 is different — it is raised by get_object_or_404() (the view helper), not by .get() directly.

mcq.q: Which lookup finds rooms where the name contains 'conf' regardless of case?
mcq.why: __icontains maps to SQL LIKE '%conf%' with case-insensitive comparison. __contains is case-sensitive. __iexact is case-insensitive but requires an exact match, not a substring.

mcq.q: How do you get the count of rooms without loading all rows into memory?
mcq.why: .count() issues SELECT COUNT(*) — a single lightweight SQL call. len(queryset) forces evaluation of the entire queryset and loads all rows into memory before counting. For large tables this is a significant performance difference.

mcq.q: What does Room.objects.all()[:5] generate in SQL?
bad: It raises an error — QuerySets don't support slicing
mcq.why: Python slice notation on a QuerySet maps directly to SQL LIMIT/OFFSET. [:5] becomes LIMIT 5. [2:7] becomes LIMIT 5 OFFSET 2. Negative slicing is not supported.

mcq.q: What is the N+1 query problem?
mcq.code:
for m in Meeting.objects.all():
    print(m.room.name)  # extra query each time
mcq.ok: Accessing a ForeignKey attribute in a loop triggers one SQL query per row, so N meetings cause N+1 total queries
bad: Calling filter() more than once on a QuerySet
Using order_by() with more than one field
mcq.why: The first query loads all meetings (1 query). Then each m.room access hits the database again for that room (N queries). Total: N+1. Fix: Meeting.objects.select_related('room').all() fetches everything in one JOIN.

mcq.q: What does .exclude(floor=1) return?
mcq.ok: All rooms where floor is NOT 1
bad: All rooms, with floor=1 rooms hidden from the template
An error — exclude() is not a valid QuerySet method
mcq.why: .exclude() is the opposite of .filter(). It returns all rows that do NOT match the given condition. It maps to SQL WHERE NOT (floor = 1).

mcq.q: What does .values('name', 'floor') return?
bad: A QuerySet of Room model instances with only those two fields
A single dict of all rooms keyed by name
mcq.why: .values() returns dictionaries, not model instances. Each dict contains only the requested fields. This avoids constructing full model objects, making it faster when you only need raw data.

mcq.q: Which ORM method bypasses model .delete() signals when removing rows?
mcq.ok: QuerySet .delete() — bulk delete at the SQL level, skipping per-object signals
bad: Both QuerySet .delete() and instance .delete() skip signals
mcq.why: QuerySet.delete() runs DELETE SQL directly without loading objects, so pre_delete and post_delete signals are not fired per object. Instance .delete() does fire signals. Use bulk delete for speed, instance delete when signals matter.

mcq.q: get_object_or_404(Room, pk=pk) — what does it raise if no Room exists with that pk?
mcq.ok: Http404 — which Django renders as a 404 Not Found page
mcq.why: get_object_or_404 catches DoesNotExist internally and re-raises it as Http404. This gives users a clean 404 page instead of a 500 server error. It's the correct tool to use in views when looking up user-supplied IDs.

mcq.q: What does .as_view() do?
mcq.ok: Converts the CBV class into a callable view function that Django can call
bad: Registers the view in Django's registry
Creates a new instance of the view class
mcq.why: Django's URL dispatcher expects a callable. CBVs are classes, not callables. .as_view() returns a function that creates an instance of the class and calls its dispatch() method on each request.

mcq.q: What is the default template name for PostListView (model=BlogPost, app='blog')?
mcq.why: Django derives the template name as <app_label>/<model_name_lower>_list.html. With app='blog' and model=BlogPost, it becomes blog/blogpost_list.html. Set template_name explicitly to use a cleaner name.

mcq.q: What is the default context variable name in a ListView when context_object_name is not set?
mcq.why: Without context_object_name, Django uses <model_name_lower>_list. For BlogPost that is 'blogpost_list'. object_list is also available as a secondary name. Set context_object_name='posts' for a cleaner template variable.

mcq.q: Why must success_url use reverse_lazy() instead of reverse()?
mcq.ok: reverse() runs at class definition time, before urls.py is loaded — raising NoReverseMatch
bad: reverse() only works in function-based views
Django requires reverse_lazy() for all URL names
mcq.why: Class attributes are evaluated when the class is defined (at import time). reverse() needs the URL conf to be loaded, but it isn't yet. reverse_lazy() defers evaluation until it's actually needed — after urls.py is loaded.

mcq.q: In which order must LoginRequiredMixin appear in the class definition?
mcq.ok: First — LoginRequiredMixin must come before CreateView
bad: It doesn't matter — Python handles it
In a separate @mixin decorator above the class
mcq.why: Python's MRO (Method Resolution Order) processes base classes left to right. LoginRequiredMixin's dispatch() must run before CreateView's dispatch(). If CreateView is listed first, the mixin's check never runs.

mcq.q: What HTTP method does DeleteView use to actually delete the object?
mcq.ok: POST — GET only shows the confirmation page
mcq.why: DeleteView on GET renders a confirmation template. On POST it calls object.delete() and redirects to success_url. This two-step process prevents accidental or CSRF-triggered deletions from a URL link.

mcq.q: Which CBV would you use to show a form pre-filled with existing data for editing?
mcq.why: UpdateView loads an existing object by pk, passes it as the initial data to the form, and UPDATE the row on POST. CreateView starts with an empty form and INSERT on POST. DetailView shows data with no editing.

mcq.q: What is the correct way to filter a ListView to only show the logged-in user's posts?
bad: Set queryset = BlogPost.objects.filter(author=request.user) as a class attribute
Pass a queryset argument to ListView.as_view()
mcq.why: Class attributes are evaluated once at import time. self.request.user doesn't exist then. get_queryset() is called on every request with self.request available. This is the correct hook for dynamic filtering.

mcq.q: What does DetailView use by default to look up the object from the URL?
mcq.ok: The pk URL keyword argument — it calls Model.objects.get(pk=pk)
mcq.why: DetailView's default pk_url_kwarg is 'pk'. It extracts pk from self.kwargs and calls get_object() which does Model.objects.get(pk=pk). To use 'id' instead, set pk_url_kwarg = 'id' on the view.

mcq.q: Which of these applies @login_required correctly to a CBV?
mcq.why: LoginRequiredMixin must be first in the class bases. Decorating the class with @login_required does not work correctly for CBVs. path(..., login_required(MyView)) also fails because MyView is not yet a callable. Use LoginRequiredMixin as first base.

mcq.q: What is the difference between User.objects.create() and User.objects.create_user()?
mcq.ok: create_user() hashes the password; create() stores it as plain text
bad: They are identical — both hash the password
mcq.why: create_user() calls set_password() which runs the password through PBKDF2 (or configured hasher). create() sets the field directly with no hashing. Never use create() for user accounts.

mcq.q: authenticate(username='malak', password='wrong') returns what?
mcq.why: authenticate() returns None when credentials don't match. It never raises an exception for wrong credentials. Always check 'if user is not None' before calling login().

mcq.q: What does login(request, user) do?
mcq.ok: Creates a session so the user stays authenticated across subsequent requests
mcq.why: login() writes the user's ID into the session. On every subsequent request, Django reads the session and sets request.user to that user. authenticate() checks credentials — login() persists the result.

mcq.q: Which built-in form handles user registration with password confirmation?
mcq.why: UserCreationForm is in django.contrib.auth.forms. It includes username, password1, and password2 fields with validation that the two passwords match and meet strength requirements.

mcq.q: What does request.user contain for a non-authenticated request?
mcq.ok: An AnonymousUser instance — is_authenticated is False
bad: An empty User object with no pk
mcq.why: Django's AuthenticationMiddleware always sets request.user. For unauthenticated requests it uses AnonymousUser, which has is_authenticated=False. It is never None — checking 'request.user != None' is always True and therefore wrong.

mcq.q: What does @login_required do when an anonymous user hits the view?
bad: Calls the view but sets request.user to None
mcq.why: @login_required checks request.user.is_authenticated. If False, it redirects to settings.LOGIN_URL (default: /accounts/login/) appending ?next= so the user is redirected back after login.

mcq.q: If LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL is not set, where does Django redirect after a successful login?
mcq.ok: /accounts/profile/ — which causes a 404 in most projects
mcq.why: Django's default LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL is '/accounts/profile/'. Since most projects don't create this URL, login succeeds but users hit a 404. Always set LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL = '/' in settings.py.

mcq.q: Which user field would you check to see if a user can access the Django admin panel?
mcq.why: is_staff=True allows access to /admin/. is_superuser=True grants all permissions (and also allows admin access). is_active=False disables the account entirely. is_authenticated checks if currently logged in.

mcq.q: What is the one-line include for all Django built-in auth views?
mcq.why: The correct string is 'django.contrib.auth.urls'. This registers login, logout, password_change, password_reset and related views under the given prefix.

mcq.q: In a template, how do you correctly check if the current user is logged in?
mcq.why: user.is_authenticated is the correct check. user != None is always True (AnonymousUser is not None). is_logged_in does not exist. request is not available as a bare name in templates (unless you pass it in context).

steps.say: Every Django app follows the same pattern: a browser sends a request, Django routes it, a view processes it, and a response comes back. Let's trace exactly what happens.
The View is the brain. It may query the database through the Model, fill a Template with the results, and return everything as an HTTP response.

Django's 'View' = MVC's Controller
Django's 'Template' = MVC's View

# pages/urls.py  (app level)

boards.title: URL routing — from browser to view

steps.say: URL routing is how Django knows which view to call when a browser visits a URL. It works in two steps: the project delegates to the app.

items: what is left to match: home/

steps.say: Here's the actual code. Notice Django strips the prefix: when pages/urls.py sees the request, the URL is just 'home/', not 'pages/home/'.

# pages/urls.py

from .views import home_page_view

urlpatterns = [
    path('home/', home_page_view, name='home'),
]

# django_project/urls.py

    path('pages/', include('pages.urls')),  # string!

steps.say: URL parameters let you capture values from the URL. The <int:id> part captures an integer and passes it as a keyword argument to the view.

# pages/urls.py
urlpatterns = [
    path('home/', home_page_view, name='home'),
    path('meeting/<int:id>/', detail_view, name='detail'),
]

# views.py
def detail_view(request, id):   # id comes from URL
    meeting = Meeting.objects.get(pk=id)
    return render(request, 'detail.html', {'meeting': meeting})

Type converters: <int:x> integers only
<str:x> any string (default)
<slug:x> letters, digits, hyphens
<uuid:x> UUID format

steps.say: The name= parameter is very powerful: it lets you reverse a URL by name instead of hardcoding the path.

{g:Advantage:} if you change the URL path from 'meeting/<int:id>/' to 'meetings/<int:pk>/', only urls.py changes — {g:all templates and Python code using the name still work}

add.q: You change path('home/', ...) to path('homepage/', ...) but keep name='home'. Does {% url 'home' %} in templates still work?
add.ok: Yes — it now generates /pages/homepage/ automatically
bad: No — you must update every template manually
No — name= must match the path string
Yes — but only if you restart the server
add.why: Named URLs reverse to whatever path() is currently set to. That's the whole point — the name is stable, the path can change.

def detail(request, id):

boards.title: on_delete — what happens when you delete the parent?
